A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VideoNSA with matching architecture and main experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-understanding evaluations, branch ablations, scaling experiments, latency measurements, and analyses of learned gates and attention sinks.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds benchmark evaluations, a static-gate ablation, context-scaling comparisons, and efficiency measurements.

M1.justification: Sections 2.1–2.3 retain the Qwen2.5-VL backbone, dense text attention, three sparse vision branches, learned gates, and training recipe. Static gates and alternative kernels appear as experimental comparisons, without replacing the proposed method.

E1.justification: Appendix G adds evaluations on LSDBench and VideoEvalPro, including the latter's holistic/local perception and reasoning categories. This extends evaluation within the existing video-understanding domain; the training data and original six benchmarks remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Tables 12–13 introduce reported comparisons with LongVA, LongVila, and Video-XL, distinct from the retained Video-XL-2. Appendix K adds Qwen2.5-VL as a comparator in context-scaling analysis, and Table 37 introduces flash-nsa versus nsa-impl. These substantially expand supplementary comparisons while preserving the original benchmark comparator sets.

E3.justification: New experimental designs include static gates averaged over a 1K training subset, dense-versus-sparse comparisons at 32K/64K/128K context, FLOPs and prefill profiling, and CMP block-size sweeps over 4K–128K contexts. Kernel forward/backward timing is compared at 8K. The original training and benchmark settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a direct static-gate ablation and benchmark-level PCA analysis of routing, dense-backbone context-scaling controls, and block-size/kernel investigations of the latency bottleneck. Appendix T also compares video and text-only NSA gating patterns. These test questions beyond v1's retained branch-removal, allocation, and sink analyses.

E5.justification: The existing gate-distribution means and interquartile summaries are retained. v2 adds no reported seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures; additional plots and point estimates do not change these reporting practices.

E6.justification: The original numerical table entries are retained, but substantial results are added: VideoNSA scores 55.2 on LSDBench and 29.4 overall on VideoEvalPro; static gating scores 31.8 versus dynamic gating's 36.1 on VSIBench. New context-scaling, training-cost, FLOPs, and kernel-latency results extend the evidence rather than establish improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

T1.justification: New Appendix M introduces a routing-stability deviation definition, mask-based mathematical reasoning about attention-budget changes, and RoPE-based extrapolation arguments incorporating a cited logit-growth bound. This substantially expands the mathematical treatment beyond v1's method and budget equations, although it supplies theoretical interpretations rather than a proved VideoNSA performance guarantee.

C1.justification: The abstract changes the relative-performance claim from 'improved' to 'competitive' against compression and training-free sparse baselines. This modestly qualifies that comparison; the introduction's contribution statements and the conclusion's main claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: New appendices attribute context-length behavior to backbone limitations and RoPE geometry, explain attention-budget sensitivity through routing disruption, and interpret gating as content-dependent and modality-specific. They also distinguish ideal computational savings from padding and kernel overheads, substantially expanding the mechanism and limitation discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix Q newly discloses padding 28 query heads to 64 for the Triton kernel and reports the dense baseline's 5280 H100 GPU hours alongside the retained 4600-hour VideoNSA figure. Implementation-specific discussion is expanded, while the existing training hyperparameters and project, code, and model access links are retained.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands citations covering video modeling and efficiency, and connects its scaling analysis to routing generalization, RoPE, LM-Infinite, and positional-encoding research. New kernel comparisons and the detailed contrast with text-only NSA broaden research positioning, while the original distinction from token-compression methods remains.

P1.justification: The main narrative and existing appendix prose are largely preserved. Changes include the conference header, the abstract qualification, updated cross-references, and an expanded appendix roadmap with inserted analytical sections. The added scientific content does not amount to a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: The appendix adds benchmark and diagnostic tables, context-scaling curves, PCA plots, efficiency charts, and text-only NSA visualizations. Existing inter-head heatmaps gain numbered captions and are regrouped, while dense-attention sink panels are consolidated. These substantially change the appendix's visual organization; the main displays are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidentiary gaps: the static-gate control directly tests dynamic routing beyond v1's branch-removal ablations, and Appendices Q–R quantify comparative efficiency and disclose implementation overheads. These substantially strengthen validation and transparency. The gains are qualified by heuristic theoretical arguments and Appendix K's overstated 128K stability: Table 27 shows declines from 64K on three benchmarks. Those weaknesses limit interpretation but do not outweigh the stronger empirical controls and cost analysis.
